Specifically, these data imply that there is an increase in oxidative stress due to elevated levels of Advanced Glycosylation End-products (AGEs) in uremic plasma.

Oxidative stress occurs when the body's antioxidant defenses are overwhelmed, leading to damage to cells and tissues. AGEs, formed through non-enzymatic glycation reactions between sugars and proteins, can accumulate in tissues and contribute to oxidative stress and inflammation.

The relationship between autoxidation products of both carbohydrates and lipids is further suggested by studies that have shown increased levels of these compounds in uremic plasma. This suggests that the oxidative stress associated with uremia may be broader than previously thought, involving alterations in both carbohydrate and lipid metabolism.

Overall, the available evidence indicates that there is an increase in autoxidation products of both carbohydrates and lipids in uremic plasma, which likely contributes to oxidative stress and inflammation, highlighting the need for further research into the mechanisms underlying this condition.
